title: Scallion Pancakes
subtitle: Cong you bing, flaky laminated flatbread layered with spring onion
excerpt: Scallion pancakes are made from a hot-water dough rolled into a thin sheet, brushed with sesame oil and salt, layered with spring onions, then rolled up, coiled and re-rolled to create a flaky laminated texture. They fry in a dry pan until crisp outside and chewy within. Makes 4 pancakes in about 60 minutes.
sourceNotes: Cong you bing, or scallion oil pancakes, are one of the oldest forms of Chinese flatbread, associated particularly with street food stalls in Shanghai and northern China. The dish is discussed in Florence Lin's 'Florence Lin's Complete Book of Chinese Noodles, Dumplings and Breads' (William Morrow, 1986) and appears in Fuchsia Dunlop's 'Every Grain of Rice' (Bloomsbury, 2012), which notes that the lamination technique of rolling, coiling and re-rolling is key to developing the characteristic flaky layers.

recipe.freezeNotes: Stack cooked pancakes between sheets of baking parchment and freeze for up to 2 months. Reheat from frozen in a dry frying pan over a medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes per side.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough can be made, rested and formed into coils, then covered in cling film and refrigerated for up to 24 hours before the final rolling and frying.

glossaryTerms.definition: A technique in which fat and dough are folded together in multiple layers to create a flaky, layered texture when cooked. In scallion pancakes the layers are created by rolling the dough thin, adding fat and filling, rolling it into a log, coiling the log and then rolling it flat again. Each step multiplies the number of layers.

Oil pressed from toasted sesame seeds, dark amber in colour and strongly flavoured. It is used as a finishing oil and flavouring rather than a cooking oil, as it burns at relatively low temperatures. In scallion pancakes a thin layer brushed onto the dough adds a nutty aroma to the layers.

A dough made by combining plain flour with boiling or very hot water, which partially cooks the starch and produces a softer, more extensible dough than cold-water dough. It rolls out more easily and stays pliable when cool, making it the standard dough for scallion pancakes, dumpling wrappers and many Chinese flatbreads.

content.text: This recipe makes 4 scallion pancakes and takes about 60 minutes including resting time. The
is more forgiving than cold-water dough and is easy to roll thinly without tearing. The rest period is important: it relaxes the gluten and makes the dough easier to handle.
step is what creates the flaky layers: roll thin, brush with
and scatter with spring onion, roll into a log, coil the log into a disc, then re-roll flat. Each coil traps oil and spring onion between the layers. Do not skip any of these steps.

Place the {{plain-flour}} and salt in a bowl. Pour in the boiling water and stir quickly with chopsticks or a fork until a shaggy dough forms. Once cool enough to handle, knead for 3 to 4 minutes until smooth. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.
Divide the rested dough into 4 equal pieces. On a lightly floured surface, roll one piece into a very thin rectangle, roughly 30cm x 20cm.
Brush the surface generously with {{sesame-oil}} and sprinkle with a little salt. Scatter a quarter of the {{spring-onions}} over the surface.
Roll the dough tightly away from you into a long log. Then coil the log into a tight disc, tucking the end underneath. Press down gently to flatten slightly. Repeat with the remaining pieces.
Roll each disc out again to a circle about 20cm across and 4 to 5mm thick. The layers will be visible as swirls in the dough.

Heat 1 tablespoon of {{vegetable-oil}} in a frying pan over a medium-high heat. Fry each pancake for 3 to 4 minutes per side until deep golden and slightly blistered. Reduce the heat if they are browning too fast. Repeat with the remaining pancakes.
Serve hot, cut into wedges. A dipping sauce of soy sauce with a little rice vinegar and sesame oil works well alongside.

items.symptom: The pancakes are tough and chewy throughout with no flaky layers
items.cause: The dough was not rested long enough, or the rolling was too thick
items.fix: Rest the dough for the full 30 minutes. Roll the rectangle as thin as you can without tearing. The layers depend on thin, tightly coiled dough.

items.symptom: The spring onion burns before the inside is cooked
items.fix: Fry over a medium rather than high heat. The pancakes need time to cook through; too much heat chars the surface before the centre warms.

items.symptom: The coil falls apart when re-rolled
items.cause: The dough was not coiled tightly enough
items.fix: Roll the log tightly and coil it firmly, pressing the end underneath with purpose. A loose coil will unwind when re-rolled rather than compressing into layers.

content.text: Scallion pancakes, known in Mandarin as cong you bing, are sold by street vendors throughout northern China and are a breakfast staple in Shanghai, where they are often eaten with warm soy milk. The lamination technique is also used in Taiwanese breakfast shops, where the pancakes are sometimes wrapped around an egg. At home they are most often eaten as a snack or a side dish with broth.
